title: The month of Asarh
hook: in Asarh the heat burns those who don't have the Lord near (Barah Maha, ang 134)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the month of Jeth, and your line: jeth: bow. Did you lower your head in the hardest moment? The heat isn't over. Asarh is the month it peaks, just before the rains. Day five hundred sixty-nine.

June into July. The fields are cracked. The canals run low. Everyone keeps looking at the sky, waiting for the monsoon, and every day the clouds gather and then don't break. People sleep on rooftops for a breath of air. The heat in Asarh isn't only on the skin; it wears on tempers, on patience, on sleep. Everyone knows someone who gets short and sharp in weather like that. Maybe it's you. Guru Arjan looked at that burning month and asked a question about it: why does the same heat feel so different to different people?
screen: `CRACKED FIELDS, WAITING FOR RAIN.` → `SLEEPING ON ROOFTOPS.` → `WHY DOES THE HEAT FEEL DIFFERENT?`

segments.voice: The Asarh stanza is on ang 134. In paraphrase: in Asarh, the heat scorches those whose Husband Lord isn't near them. Then he says why. They've left the One who is the life of the world, and put their hope in mortal people. Caught up in duality, in what is second, they're ruined, and death's noose is around their neck. As they sow, so they reap; what is written comes to pass. Then a picture of a whole life passing like a night: the night slips by, she regrets it, and she leaves without hope. And then the turn: Asarh is pleasant, the stanza says, for the one in whose heart the Lord's feet dwell. Same month. Same heat. For one person it's a furnace, for another it's bearable, even pleasant. The difference isn't the weather. It's what's near. There's a careful line in the middle worth slowing on: they put their hope in mortal people. Guru Arjan isn't saying don't rely on anyone. Sikh life is built on sangat, community. The problem is resting your whole hope on people who are themselves passing, who will get tired and short in the heat too. When everything you lean on is also burning, there's nowhere cool to stand. Notice also the line about sowing and reaping. In a farming month, waiting for rain, everyone knows a harvest is the fruit of what was planted. Guru Arjan uses that knowledge plainly: a life gives back what was sown. And the stanza's cool center is still the same image: the Lord's feet dwelling in the heart. Keep the One near, and the heat changes.
screen: `THE HEAT BURNS THOSE FAR FROM THE ONE.` · `HOPE IN MORTALS, WHO ALSO BURN.` · `AS YOU SOW, SO YOU REAP.` · `THE LORD'S FEET IN THE HEART.` · then, large: `ASARH: KEEP HIM NEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: cool someone down. Sit and breathe slowly, imagining cool air on the out-breath. Then think of someone in your life who's running hot right now: stressed, short-tempered, overwhelmed. Don't judge their heat. Picture bringing them something cool: a glass of water, a calm word, ten minutes of help, simply not adding to their pressure. Choose one small, concrete thing you can actually do today. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them. The bell holds the time.
The month of Asarh. The peak of the heat: it scorches those far from the One, and is pleasant for the one in whose heart the Lord's feet dwell.
Your line: asarh: keep him near. Today, bring your cool thing to the person you pictured, and when you feel your own temper heating, breathe out slowly once. Day five hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: On the sangrand of Asarh, many gurdwaras read the Asarh stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, and the sangat hears it as the hottest stretch of the year gives way to the rains.

fork.setup: two people sit through the same burning Asarh afternoon. one is miserable, one is at peace. what does the stanza say makes the difference?
options: the Lord's feet dwell in one's heart.
fork.reveal: Asarh is pleasant for the one in whose heart the Lord's feet dwell. the heat scorches those whose Lord isn't near.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Asarh, the month of peak heat before the monsoon.

trapdoor: what you thought: a poem about a hot month.
what it means: the same heat burns or doesn't depending on what's near the heart; hope resting only on passing people burns too.
what a scholar hears: 'aasaarh tapandaa tis lagai har naahu na jinaa paas'; the stanza moves from scorching heat to sowing and reaping to the night of life slipping by.

sources.ref: Barah Maha, Majh M5, Asarh stanza, Ang 134

notes: Asarh stanza paraphrased; confirm content (heat scorches those without the Husband Lord near; abandoning the Life of the world, hoping in mortals; ruined in duality, noose of death; as one sows so one reaps; night passes, she regrets and departs without hope; Asarh pleasant for one with the Lord's feet in the heart).
Gurmukhi spelling ਆਸਾੜੁ as in the stanza's first word; confirm.
Interpretive point about sangat (relying on people is not condemned; resting all hope on mortals is) is the narrator's framing; confirm.
